My family has farmed this land in Quzhou my whole life. My father grew wheat and corn, and I've done the same for thirty years. I know what works here. The soil is good, the water table is reachable, and the markets are nearby. I'm not going to experiment at my age — I'll do what I know.

I have 8 mu. All of it goes into wheat in winter and corn in summer. That's the only sensible thing. You plant wheat in October, harvest in June, then immediately put corn in. The land doesn't rest — I can't afford for it to.

For wheat I buy the improved seeds from the village shop, the kind the township office has been pushing for years. Yields are better than the old seeds my father saved. I put down compound fertilizer when I plant, then I top-dress with urea in spring when the wheat wakes up from the cold. I water four times — before the ground freezes, again in March, again when the stalks are shooting up, and once more when the grain is filling out. I spray for weeds early and for rust and aphids when I see them or when my neighbors start spraying.

For corn, everyone uses hybrid seeds now. I get whatever Zhengdan variety they have at the shop — it's been reliable. I apply less fertilizer than wheat because the summer rains help. I usually water once or twice depending on how dry July gets. Corn is easier. I can manage it without thinking too hard.

I don't keep written records. I know what a healthy crop looks like and I follow the rhythm of the village.
